key_findings.title: Vipassana practice has a distinct EEG signature
key_findings.text: Meditators show distinct combinations of periodic and aperiodic EEG activity (a marker of excitation/inhibition balance), and meditation is distinct from the sleep state.

key_findings.title: Each meditation tradition has its own EEG signature
key_findings.text: Brahma Kumaris: similar periodic and slower aperiodic activity. Isha Yoga: slower periodic and faster aperiodic. Heartfulness: slower periodic and similar aperiodic. Vipassana shows its own combination.

key_findings.title: Meditation practice enhances deep and REM sleep
key_findings.text: Whole-night polysomnography shows enhanced slow-wave sleep with Sudarshan Kriya Yoga, and enhanced slow-wave and REM sleep with Vipassana.
key_findings.citation: Sulekha et al., Sleep and Biological Rhythms (2006) 4:207-214

key_findings.title: Meditation attenuates age-associated changes in slow-wave sleep
key_findings.text: Vipassana practitioners keep enhanced slow-wave and REM sleep across age groups, while controls lose slow-wave sleep with age.
key_findings.citation: Ravindra et al., Sleep and Biological Rhythms (2010), 34-41

key_findings.title: Meditation and sleep-regulating hormones
key_findings.text: Meditators have higher melatonin levels, and DHEA levels correlate positively with the share of N3 (deep) sleep.

key_findings.title: REM sleep micro-architecture in meditators
key_findings.text: Senior meditators show more phasic REM events, higher REM density and longer REM bursts, with less N2 and wake after sleep onset and more deep sleep.
key_findings.citation: Nirmala et al., International Review of Psychiatry (2016)

key_findings.title: Meditation mitigates age-related decline in spindle integrity
key_findings.text: Age-related decline in sleep-spindle oscillations is weaker in meditators (r = -0.29) than in controls (r = -0.45).

key_findings.title: How long-term Vipassana practice reshapes sleep
key_findings.text: Long-term practice is linked to refined sleep spindles, denser REM sleep, more slow-wave and REM sleep with less N2, and a more resilient, restorative sleep state.

key_findings.title: Ayurvedic treatment preserves deep sleep; clonazepam suppresses it
key_findings.text: Slow-wave sleep was 20.5% with Ayurvedic treatment versus 7.2% with clonazepam: restorative deep sleep is preserved with Ayurveda and significantly suppressed with clonazepam.

key_findings.title: Failed sleep homeostasis in schizophrenia: chemical
key_findings.text: Higher evening ADA (adenosine deaminase) levels correlate with positive symptoms such as auditory hallucinations; the evening-to-morning difference trends towards a negative correlation with avolition-apathy.
key_findings.citation: Sasidharan et al., Asian Journal of Psychiatry (2017)

key_findings.title: Failed sleep homeostasis in schizophrenia: architecture
key_findings.text: Patients' sleep is fragmented: 330% longer sleep onset latency, 16% lower sleep efficiency, 256% more wake after sleep onset and 48% more stage transitions.

key_findings.title: Failed sleep homeostasis in schizophrenia: oscillations
key_findings.text: Spindle deficits in one NREM period are positively correlated with awakenings in the following REM period, suggesting a causal link between failing spindles and sleep-cycle instability.

key_findings.title: Inducing lucidity in dreams
key_findings.text: Cognitive training plus auditory cues induced lucid dreams in 5 of 6 trained participants (83.3%) versus 1 of 5 untrained controls (20%).
key_findings.citation: Gulshan et al., International Journal of Dream Research (2018)

key_findings.title: Decoding dream content
key_findings.text: A rise in beta-band power (15-30 Hz) was the key electrophysiological feature preceding successful dream recall, in both N2 and REM sleep.

key_findings.title: Shaping dream content
key_findings.text: 10.42% of auditory cues were directly incorporated into the next dream report; targeted memory reactivation cut sadness in dreams from 33.3% to 4.5%.
